question.problem: Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x)=9{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-x-1$ have multiplicity $1?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. For this polynomial, we can factor by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =9{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-x-1 \\  & =9{x}^{2}(x+1)-1(x+1) \\  & =(9{x}^{2}-1)(x+1) \\  & =(3x+1)(3x-1)(x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

- The factor $(3x+1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-\frac{1}{3}$ has multiplicity $1.$

- The factor $(3x-1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=\frac{1}{3}$ has multiplicity $1.$

- The factor $(x+1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-1$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, the roots $x=-1,\,-\frac{1}{3},\,\frac{1}{3}$ all have multiplicity $1.$
